newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists cling to power despite rallies.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists cling to power despite rallies.

text.p: Bulgaria's ex-communist Socialists clung doggedly to power on Tuesday, insisting they would form a new government despite daily opposition rallies and a presidential appeal for general elections.
Sofia students staged their biggest rally to date, marching to the Socialist headquarters with soap and towels to mock the party's "clean hands" initiative to stop rampant corruption.
The three main trade unions called a general strike from Wednesday to protest against the deepening economic crisis and back opposition calls for immediate elections.

Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the Socialists' nominee for premier, said after meeting President Petar Stoyanov he sympathised with the protesters and planned a cabinet of non-party technocrats to rescue the economy.

"I extend my hand to all Bulgarians, to all political forces, and I insist that together we should work out an anti-crisis programme," said Dobrev, who was jeered by about 100 protesters outside the presidency.
The opposition has held daily rallies since January 6 to demand the removal of the Socialist government, which won elections in December 1994.

About 10,000 students, blowing whistles and rattling cans filled with worthless coins, marched to the Socialist headquarters behind a banner reading "I'm not a slave, what about you?" Police and journalists said it was the biggest demonstration they had seen.
Thousands more demonstrators gathered outside the Alexander Nevsky cathedral for the opposition's main daily rally.
Trade union officials said the strike would start at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT). Evening rallies are faithfully attended, but one-hour warning strikes this month have had limited support.
Four army and police officers' associations issued an appeal for calm, saying they opposed any use of force against unarmed civilians.
A police union spokesman said many police earned only 15,000 levs ($15) per month and were as badly off as the protesters.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov was obliged to ask the Socialists as the biggest party in parliament to form a cabinet, but on Monday he appealed to them to refuse the mandate and agree to opposition demands for early elections.

"I hope they realise their huge responsibility if they carry out a mandate to form a cabinet which is already rejected by society," Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces told reporters.
The opposition holds Dobrev responsible for clashes between demonstrators and police after protesters besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10.

Dobrev has a week to name his cabinet, which must be voted on by parliament. The opposition is pinning its hopes on defections from the divided ruling party, which has 125 seats in the 240-seat legislature.

The collapsing currency slipped below 1,000 levs to the dollar on the interbank market for the first time and dealers said they expected more falls. Banks had to call in technicians to reset their software to accept four-digit quotes.
At the beginning of January, the central bank daily fix was 495.74 levs to the dollar.

The Socialists' youth wing said it planned a counter-demonstration on Friday outside the headquarters of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces in Sofia to protest at what organisers describe as "UDF manipulation".
"I think that the Socialists are clearly looking for a clash but they will not get one on Friday," said student protest organiser Borislav Borislavov.
He said the students would respond by holding their daily rally outside the Socialist headquarters on Friday.
